name: Van Dyke beard

lead: The Van Dyke is a facial hair style made of a moustache and a goatee that are not joined, with the cheeks and jaw shaved. Because the hair is concentrated on the upper lip and chin, it frames the mouth and draws the eye down the centre of the face.

The style is named for the Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck, who depicted it in the 17th century. It is a style choice rather than a medical or surgical intervention, so published research on it specifically is essentially absent; what exists is historical and cultural documentation.

paras: Wearers grow hair on the upper lip and chin, then shave the cheeks and the area connecting the two. The goatee is typically kept pointed and the moustache is trimmed neat or waxed and curled, which are the two common variants. Many men also add or omit a soul patch. Upkeep is frequent trimming and edging.

The style carries the ordinary risks of shaving and trimming, such as razor irritation and ingrown hairs. Facial hair growth pattern varies between men, and patchy growth around the mouth can make the separated shapes harder to achieve.

angle.text: The style adds visible structure around the mouth and chin using facial hair alone. Wearers use it to emphasise a chin or to give the lower face a deliberately groomed outline.

lead: The Van Dyke beard is a facial hair style consisting of a moustache and a goatee with the cheeks shaved, the two parts left disconnected.[1] Variants include a curled or uncurled moustache and versions with or without a soul patch.[1]

People adopt it as a grooming choice to give the lower face more structure: the pointed goatee extends the visual length of the chin, while the shaved cheeks leave the jawline outline visible. Forum users on T Nation have discussed moustache and goatee styling in threads about grooming and facial hair.[2][3]
The style is named for the Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck (1599-1641), who painted it and wore it himself.[1] It is also called a Charlie, after King Charles I, and a pike-devant.[1]

paras: The look pairs a moustache with a goatee on the chin and leaves a shaved gap between them, with no hair on the cheeks.[1] The goatee is usually kept to a point, and the moustache may be left natural, trimmed short or waxed into curls.[1]

The style was popular in 17th-century Europe and takes its name from van Dyck, who portrayed sitters wearing it.[1] In Britain it declined after the Restoration in 1660, when French fashions and wigs took over, although some wearers of so-called vow-beards kept it going.[1] It returned to the United States in the 19th century, when a Chicago columnist writing between 1895 and 1908 criticised it along with the goatee.[1]

Wikipedia lists Charles I, Vladimir Lenin, General Custer, Monty Woolley, Colonel Sanders, Jonathan Hyde and John Hurt among notable wearers, and its gallery also shows Rudolph Valentino, Johnny Depp, Christian Bale and Pierce Brosnan.[1]

Moustaches and goatees come up in general men's grooming discussions on T Nation, including threads on moustaches and on styling in hair loss.[2][3][4] Participants in such threads trade views on what suits their own face and growth patterns.
